You turn verbs and adjectives into nouns, write headlines and press releases in the nominal style, and replace subordinate clauses with noun phrases in formal writing.
After your arrival, we’ll go and see the house.
The match was cancelled because of the rain.
Know the irregular nouns (naissance, mort, départ, vente, choix, perte).
Turn a whole sentence into a nominal headline.
Replace a subordinate clause with a noun phrase (après son départ, en raison de, pour la rénovation).
Friday, 24 February 2033, evening, in Bucharest. Mr Ciobanu, director of the Arhimar firm, has written the press release for the next day’s signing. He calls Ioana to read it to her.
Ioana, I’ve written the press release. Listen: “We are delighted to announce that we are going to save a magnificent house and that we are going to create a music school in it!”
It’s enthusiastic. But journalists want short headlines. You need to switch to the nominal style.
You replace the verbs with nouns. “We are going to save a house” becomes “Rescue of a historic house”.
And “we are going to create a school”?
“Creation of a music school”. And “we are signing an agreement” becomes “Signing of a European agreement”.
That sounds very administrative, doesn’t it?
For the headline, yes. It’s made to be read in three seconds. Afterwards, in the text, you can put verbs back in.
All right. And the date? I wrote “when the work starts, in September”.
Write instead: “Work begins in September”. And for “when the school opens”: “Opening planned for 2035”.
You’re formidable. And Mrs Stan, how do I introduce her?
“Owner of the house since her birth, in 1940.” No verb needed.
And to finish? I had put: “We thank everyone because they helped us.”
“Thanks to all our partners for their support.” There. Your press release is ready.
(he laughs) It’s perfect. But it’s a bit sad, without verbs.
We’ll keep the verbs for tomorrow. For the real story.
In the nominal style, the main idea is carried by a NOUN, not a verb. It is the style of newspaper headlines, press releases, notes, CVs and administrative texts:
On va sauver une maison historique.
The verb’s object becomes the noun’s complement, introduced by “de”: “sauver la maison” → “le sauvetage de la maison”. The agent is introduced by “par”: “signature de l’accord par la fondation”.
2. From verb to noun: the suffixes
créer → la création, rénover → la rénovation
lancer → le lancement, classer → le classement
nettoyer → le nettoyage, sauver → le sauvetage
Gender tip: -tion, -ure, -ée are almost always feminine; -ment and -age are almost always masculine (exceptions: la page, l’image, la plage).
rapide → la rapidité, efficace → l’efficacité, transparent → la transparence (!)
sage → la sagesse, jeune → la jeunesse, faible → la faiblesse
grand → la grandeur, épais → l’épaisseur, lent → la lenteur
certain → la certitude, seul → la solitude
Nouns in -eur formed from adjectives are FEMININE: la grandeur, la lenteur, la largeur. Don’t confuse them with the -eur of professions (le chanteur).
Many very common verbs have nouns that follow no rule. They must be learnt by heart:
Romanian does this too: “a pleca → plecarea”, “a vinde → vânzarea”. But French has more irregular forms, especially with short verbs.
In formal writing, a heavy subordinate clause can be replaced by a preposition + noun. The sentence becomes shorter and more elegant:
pour la rénovation de la maison
Don’t overdo it! A whole text in the nominal style becomes hard to read, like an administrative report. Use it in headlines, notes and key sentences, but keep verbs for the story.
“Le ministre a démissionné.” in the nominal style:
Que veulent les journalistes, selon Ioana ?
Que devient « nous signons un accord » ?
Depuis quand Madame Stan est-elle propriétaire ?

The house behind Piața Romană belonged to a single person: the old lady on the bench. Her name was Viorica Stan. She was ninety-two. She had been born in that house in 1940, on the first floor, in the room overlooking the wave-shaped balcony. Her father was a piano teacher at the Bucharest Conservatoire. Her mother translated French novels. The house had been built by her grandfather in 1907.

In 1950 the house had been confiscated by the communist regime and divided into six flats. The Stan family had been allowed to keep a single room on the ground floor. The piano had been left on the first floor, with a family of workers who used it as a table. After the fall of the regime in 1989, it had taken Viorica twelve years to get the house back. But she had never had the money to repair it.

Ioana had learnt all this by phone over the winter, calling Viorica every Sunday. Mr Ciobanu had found her number through the land registry. The old lady spoke an old-fashioned Romanian, elegant, full of French words. She told her life in pieces, one week after another, like a serial. Ioana took notes. By the end of the winter she knew the story of every room in the house.

There was a problem. Viorica’s three grandchildren, who lived in London, Madrid and Toronto, wanted to sell the house. A property developer had made them a very generous offer. He wanted to demolish it and build an eight-storey block in its place, with offices and luxury flats. The land was worth a fortune. The house, according to the developer, was worth nothing.

Only Ilinca, the granddaughter in Madrid, hesitated. She taught violin at a Spanish conservatoire, and had spent all the summers of her childhood in the house, listening to her grandmother talk about the piano. She had written Viorica a long letter in Romanian, with spelling mistakes that made the old lady smile. In it she said she didn’t want to sell. But that she didn’t have the means to stand up to her two brothers.

Viorica refused. But she was ninety-two, and knew very well that the decision would slip out of her hands sooner or later. “After my death,” she had told Ioana one Sunday, “they’ll sell. I don’t hold it against them. They have their lives over there. But I’d like the house to be saved before that. So that it can no longer be destroyed.” Ioana had thought about it all week. Then she had called Julien, and Mr Ciobanu, and Amina.

The project they had built together, throughout January, fitted into one sentence: turning the house into a music school for the neighbourhood children, while leaving Viorica her ground-floor flat for life. The renovation would be done by Arhimar and the Fabre & Popescu firm. The funding would come from a European heritage foundation. And the lessons would be organised on the “Musique en partage” model.

Amina had done the budget in three days. It was perfectly balanced. But the foundation’s file required one condition: the house had to be listed as a historic monument by the Romanian state. Without that listing, no funding. And without funding, no rescue. So Ioana had spent her January evenings writing, in Romanian, an eighty-page listing application, with plans, photos and the complete history of the house.

One Sunday in January, Viorica had told her about her father’s last lesson. It was March 1950, the day before the confiscation. He had called his six pupils into the drawing room, one by one, and had each of them play the same piece: a little Chopin waltz. Then he had locked the piano. He had put the key in the pocket of his daughter, who was ten. Viorica still had that key.

Julien, for his part, had presented the project to the network’s board. It would be the first “Musique en partage” school outside France. The board had hesitated: the network was funded by French public money, and could not pay for Bucharest. Amina had settled the question in one sentence. The network would not give money. It would give its method. And a method, she pointed out, did not appear on any budget line.

Meanwhile, in Lyon, Nathalie was leaving her more and more responsibilities. Ioana now chaired the Monday meetings, signed quotes and received clients. She learnt fast. Above all she learnt to delegate, which was the hardest part. Hugo worked from home on Fridays and had never been so efficient. The two interns he was training were making spectacular progress. The firm had never done so well.

The reply from the Romanian Ministry of Culture arrived on 3 February 2033. Ioana read it at the office at eight in the morning, trembling. The Stan house was officially listed as a historic monument, “on account of the exceptional quality of its Art Nouveau façade and its importance in the city’s musical history”. Ioana printed the letter, read it three times and called Viorica. Viorica cried on the phone.

In Lyon, at the firm, the news went round the offices in five minutes. Sophie, the accountant, brought out a bottle of crémant she kept for big occasions. Karim put Romanian jazz on the speakers. Hugo printed a photo of the façade and stuck it on the meeting-room door. And Nathalie, who never drank at the office, raised her glass and said simply: “To the bridge.”

The listing changed everything. The house could no longer be demolished. The developer withdrew his offer within the week. And the European foundation confirmed the funding on 14 February, Valentine’s Day, which Amina judged “unrelated, but statistically interesting”. The signing of the agreement was set for Saturday 25 February in Bucharest, during the children’s winter holidays. The whole family decided to make the trip.

They left Lyon on Thursday 23 February: Ioana, Julien, Rose-Hélène and Henri-Ion, who was flying for the first time and spent the whole flight trying to open the window. Elena, Dan and Grandma came from Iași by train the same day. Grandma had refused to fly this time. She said once was enough to talk with God, and that he shouldn’t be disturbed too often.

At Bucharest airport, Mr Ciobanu was waiting for them himself, with a bouquet of flowers for Ioana and two enormous lollipops for the children. He drove the whole family to the hotel, talking non-stop, pointing out monuments, explaining the history of every street. Henri-Ion fell asleep after ten minutes, lollipop in hand. Rose-Hélène listened to the end, very seriously, without understanding a single word.

In the evening, Ioana went to fetch her mother, father and grandmother from the Gara de Nord. The Iași train was two hours late. Grandma got off first, with her icon, her cool box and a bag of plăcinte for Viorica, whom she didn’t yet know. She looked at the station, the neon lights, the crowd. Then she said Bucharest had become too big, and that she preferred Lyon, where at least you knew your neighbours.

Later, while Julien was putting the children to bed, Ioana and Elena went for a walk in Cișmigiu park under the street lamps. The lake was frozen. Elena took her daughter’s arm. They walked for a long time without speaking. Then Elena said, very quietly, that she had been sad when Ioana turned down the job. But that reading the newspapers, seeing her daughter’s name next to a historic monument, she had been proud. Very proud.

On Friday morning, Ioana took the whole family to see the house. It was cold, a dry, bright February cold. The street was quiet. The house stood there between two modern buildings, like an old lady between two teenagers. The façade was grey with dust. The wave-shaped balcony was rusty. But under the dust you could still make out the carved flowers, the rounded windows, the supple lines of Art Nouveau.

Dan, who had bought a new camera for the occasion, photographed everything. The façade, the balcony, the windows, the pigeons, his wife, his daughter, his grandchildren, and even a dustbin which, according to him, had “beautiful light”. Elena asked him to stop after a hundred photos. He took a hundred and fifty more. He said that in twenty years, when the school was full of children, someone would want to know what it had been like before.

Viorica was waiting for them on the bench, as always, with a bag of seed for the pigeons. She wore a very old black coat, a veiled hat and grey leather gloves. She stood up when she saw Ioana arriving, slowly, leaning on her cane. The two women had met only once, in October. But after all those Sundays on the phone, they embraced like two old friends.

Then Viorica saw Grandma. The two old ladies looked at each other for a long time, in silence, on the pavement. One had grown up in a house of musicians in Bucharest. The other had grown up on a farm near Iași, without electricity. There were six years between them. They had lived through the same century, the same war, the same regime, from two different sides of life. Grandma held out her hand. Viorica took it in both of hers.

“You’re the grandmother who whistles,” said Viorica. “Ioana has told me about you.” Grandma replied that she had only been whistling since last summer, and only at night, when nobody could hear. Viorica laughed. She said that in her home, long ago, everyone played an instrument except her. Her father had declared her “deaf from birth” at the age of five. She had spent her life listening to others.

Viorica took an enormous iron key out of her bag, even older than Nathalie’s, and opened the front door. The door resisted, then gave way with a terrible creak. Inside it was dark and cold. It smelled of damp, dust and time. Wallpaper hung in shreds, the parquet was smashed, the windows were boarded up. Henri-Ion hid behind his father’s legs.

They went up to the first floor by a wooden staircase that creaked at every step. Viorica went first, very slowly, holding the banister. She stopped on every landing to catch her breath and tell them something. Here, her father gave his lessons. There, her mother translated Proust at night, by candlelight. There again, in 1956, she had received her first kiss, from an architecture student who had left for America.

On the first floor, in the big room overlooking the balcony, stood the piano. A huge black grand piano, covered in a layer of dust so thick it looked like grey felt. One of the legs was broken and replaced by a pile of bricks. The lid was closed. On the lid, someone had carved, a very long time ago, with the point of a knife: “Ion + Maria 1971”.

Viorica went up to the piano. She laid her gloved hand on the lid, very gently, like on the head of an old dog. “My father played it until 1950,” she said. “After that, nobody ever opened it again. Or only to carve hearts on it.” She smiled. She said the workers who had lived here were good people. They had simply needed a table. You couldn’t hold it against them.

Rose-Hélène had come closer too. She was almost five and had never seen a grand piano. She asked if she could open the lid. Viorica looked at Ioana, then nodded. Julien helped his daughter lift the lid. Underneath, the keys were yellowed, some were missing, others were broken. Rose-Hélène pressed a white key in the middle of the keyboard. Nothing. Silence.

She pressed another key. Still nothing. Then a third, a little further to the right. And this time a sound came out. A strange sound, out of tune, hoarse, coming from very far away, like a voice waking after a long sleep. It echoed through the big empty room, against the bare walls, under the cracked ceiling. Viorica closed her eyes. She said, very softly: “That’s an A. My father always started with the A.”

In the afternoon, while the adults discussed the work, Rose-Hélène and Henri-Ion stayed on the bench with Viorica to feed the pigeons. Viorica taught them to put the seeds on the back of their hand and keep perfectly still. After five minutes, a grey pigeon landed on Rose-Hélène’s wrist. She didn’t move. She didn’t even breathe. Viorica said it was patience that made musicians.

On Saturday morning, Viorica had spent an hour searching the drawers of her little flat for her mother’s bottle of violet ink. She had found it at the bottom of a shoebox, among letters and photos. The ink dated from 1962. It had half dried up. Viorica had added a few drops of water, shaken it, and tried her old pen on a scrap of paper. The ink still flowed. She had smiled.

On Saturday 25 February, at eleven o’clock, the signing of the agreement took place in Arhimar’s big meeting room, on the top floor of the glass tower. There were Mr Ciobanu, the representative of the European foundation, a deputy mayor of Bucharest, three journalists, Ioana, Julien and, seated in the front row in her black coat, Viorica Stan, who had insisted on signing herself, with a dip pen, in her mother’s violet ink.

The European foundation’s representative, a very tall Dutchman named Mr Van Dijk, gave a short speech in English. He said his foundation had saved two hundred buildings in twenty years, but that it was the first time a listing file had arrived with the history of every room, handwritten by an architect, over twenty Sundays on the phone. He looked at Ioana. She went bright red.

After the signing, the journalists surrounded Viorica. They wanted to know how she felt. She thought, her pen still in her hand, violet ink on her fingers. Then she answered that at ninety-two, you didn’t feel much that was new any more. But that this morning, for the first time since 1950, she had wanted to buy flowers for the house. The journalists wrote it down. It was the sentence that would appear in every article.

Mr Ciobanu had prepared a press release. He had had Ioana reread it the evening before, by phone, and they had spent an hour rewriting it. Mr Ciobanu wrote the way he spoke, with lots of verbs and enthusiasm. Ioana had taught him to write like the newspapers: with nouns. “Rescue of a historic house. Creation of a music school. Signing of a European agreement.” Mr Ciobanu had found it cold. Then efficient.

The next day, the Bucharest newspapers picked up the press release almost word for word. “Rebirth of the Stan house: a music school to open in 2035”, ran one headline. “Franco-Romanian collaboration to rescue an Art Nouveau gem”, ran another. The third had chosen a simpler headline, with a photo of Viorica signing with her pen: “The lady on the bench has won”. It was Viorica’s favourite.

That same Saturday, a man of about forty arrived at the end of the ceremony, out of breath, a travel bag in his hand. It was Andrei, Viorica’s grandson, who lived in London. He had heard the news the day before and taken the first plane. He was furious. He said nobody had consulted him, that the house belonged to the family too, that his grandmother was no longer in a fit state to make that kind of decision.

There was an embarrassed silence in the room. The journalists took out their notebooks. Mr Ciobanu went pale. Ioana stood up to reply, but Viorica stopped her with a gesture. She stood up in turn, slowly, leaning on her cane. She looked at her grandson. Then she said, in a perfectly clear voice: “Andrei. Sit down. I’m going to tell you a story I’ve never told you.”

And in front of everyone, she told it. The house confiscated in 1950. Her father, driven out of the Conservatoire, who ended his life as a night watchman in a factory. The piano turned into a table. The twelve years of lawsuits to get the house back. The thirty years spent on the bench opposite, waiting. Then she said: “Your great-grandfather could never go home. I could. I want other children to be able to go in after me. That’s all.”

Andrei said nothing. He sat down. He stayed a long time with his head bowed, elbows on his knees. Then he asked to see the house. Viorica took him there that very afternoon, with Ioana and the whole family. He hadn’t been inside since he was ten. He climbed the creaking staircase. He went into the big room. He stopped in front of the piano, in front of the hearts carved on the lid.

Rose-Hélène, who didn’t understand the adults’ Romanian but understood faces very well, went up to him. She took her harmonica out of her pocket. She played the three notes, very softly, in the big cold room. Andrei looked at her, surprised. Then, without thinking, he reached for the keyboard and pressed a key. The only one that worked. The A. The old hoarse sound answered the harmonica.

Viorica put her hand to her mouth. She said, in Romanian, that it was exactly her father’s gesture. Andrei smiled for the first time that day. He said he had taken piano lessons in London for six years as a child, and had given it all up as a teenager. He couldn’t play anything any more. Viorica replied that it didn’t matter at all. The house remembered for him.

Leaving the house, Andrei called his sister in Madrid and his brother in Toronto, on the pavement, in front of everyone. He talked for a long time, in English, pacing up and down. Ilinca cried on the phone with relief. The brother in Toronto asked how much money they would lose. Andrei answered: a lot. Then he added that they would gain something no developer could ever sell them. The brother hung up without answering. He called back an hour later to say yes.

That evening, Andrei had dinner with the whole family in a little restaurant near Piața Romană. He talked for a long time with Ioana, in a mix of English and Romanian, about the work, the schedule, the budget. He asked precise questions. He was an engineer with a construction company in London. At the end of the meal, he offered to follow the work as a volunteer, remotely, and to come to Bucharest once a month. Ioana accepted.

That evening, in the little ground-floor flat where Viorica had lived alone for forty years, Grandma and Viorica stayed talking until midnight. Nobody knows exactly what they said to each other. Elena, who came to fetch Grandma at a quarter past midnight, found them sitting side by side on the old sofa, a box of photos open between them, laughing like two schoolgirls.

On Sunday morning, Grandma and Viorica went to church together, in a little Orthodox church in the neighbourhood, two streets from the house. Viorica hadn’t been inside for years; her legs could no longer carry her that far. That morning, Grandma held her arm the whole way. They each lit two candles. Nobody found out who the four candles were for. They didn’t tell anyone.

At noon, a piano restorer came to examine the grand piano, sent by Mr Ciobanu. He was a small bald man named Mr Petrescu, who had restored the pianos of the Romanian Athenaeum. He spent an hour on all fours under the instrument with a torch, muttering. Then he got up, covered in dust. He said the soundboard was intact. It would take two years. But the piano would sing again.

On Sunday, before leaving, Viorica asked for one last thing. She wanted to open the balcony door. The wave door. She hadn’t opened it since 1950. The balcony was rusty, the door was stuck, and Andrei said it was dangerous. But Viorica insisted. So Julien and Andrei pushed together, as hard as they could, while Ioana held the old lady by the arm.

The door burst open in a cloud of dust and rust. The cold February air came into the room. And Viorica Stan, ninety-two years old, stepped forward to the threshold of the balcony, without setting foot on it, and looked at the street. Her street. The bench opposite. The pigeons. The Bucharest sky above the rooftops. She said nothing for a long time. She was breathing.

In the street, passers-by stopped. An old woman, a delivery man on a bike, two students. They were looking at that door, open for the first time in so long that they had always thought it was sealed. A neighbour on the second floor of the building opposite opened her window. She shouted in Romanian: “Doamna Stan! Is that you?” Viorica raised her hand to greet her. The neighbour applauded.

Then Rose-Hélène slipped between the adults’ legs, right to the edge of the threshold, next to Viorica. She looked at the street, the passers-by, the neighbour at her window. Then she took out her harmonica and played the three notes, as loudly as she could, towards the street. The old woman below smiled. The delivery man whistled something that sounded like nothing at all. The two students applauded.

And behind them, in the big room, Grandma whistled the next three notes. Loudly this time. Off-key, but loudly. In front of everyone. Elena turned round, astonished. Dan dropped his camera. Grandma shrugged. She said she was eighty-seven, she was in Bucharest, and if the devil wanted to come, he was welcome: there was a music school to build, and they would need hands.

On the flight home, Henri-Ion fell asleep straight away, exhausted. Rose-Hélène was looking out of the window. Ioana was rereading the press release, printed and folded in her bag, with its headlines full of nouns. “Rescue. Creation. Signing.” She thought the newspapers were right, in a way: the nouns said what had been done. But the verbs were missing. The ones that said how.

So she took out a notebook and wrote, for herself, the version with the verbs. “An old lady waited thirty years on a bench. A little girl played three notes. An angry man sat down. A door opened. A grandmother whistled in front of everyone.” She reread both versions. Then she kept both. The nouns were needed for the newspapers. And the verbs, to remember.

On Monday, in Lyon, Ioana put a framed photo on her desk that Dan had sent her during the night. It showed Viorica on the threshold of the wave balcony, her hand raised towards the street, and Rose-Hélène beside her, harmonica to her lips. Hugo stopped in front of the photo. He asked who the old lady was. Ioana answered: “Our first client in Bucharest.” Then she corrected herself: “Our first friend.”

The following Sunday, as every Sunday since the autumn, Ioana called Viorica. The old lady picked up at the first ring. She said she was well. That she had bought flowers, yellow tulips, and put them in the big room, on the piano. Then she added something Ioana never forgot: “I haven’t closed the balcony door again. I’m leaving it open. It does you good, an open door.”
Qu’est-ce qui a sauvé la maison de la démolition ?
Quelle touche du piano fonctionne encore ?

The final press release, rewritten by Mr Ciobanu with Ioana’s help. Notice the nominal headlines and the body text, which keeps its verbs. Listen to the text twice, then read it aloud. At the end, answer 4 questions.
Communiqué de presse : Renaissance de la maison Stan
Bucharest, 25 February 2033. Signing of a European agreement to rescue the Stan house, an Art Nouveau gem built in 1907 behind Piața Romană.
Listing as a historic monument: 3 February. Funding: a European heritage foundation. Project management: the Arhimar firm, in collaboration with the Lyon firm Fabre & Popescu.
Creation of a free music school for the neighbourhood children, on the model of the French network “Musique en partage”. Start of work: September 2033. Planned opening: September 2035.

Mrs Viorica Stan, owner of the house since her birth in 1940, will keep her ground-floor flat. After the confiscation of the house in 1950 and twelve years of proceedings to recover it, she turned down several offers from property developers.
“My father taught piano in this house,” says Mrs Stan. “I want children to learn music here after me.” The family piano, forgotten since 1950, will be restored.
Thanks to all partners for their support, and in particular to Mrs Stan for her patience and trust.
Quand la maison Stan a-t-elle été construite ?
Creation of a free music school.
